content: In a study conducted among young adults during 1986-1987, the inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV) demonstrated a 75% reduction in influenza A (H1N1) illness during the first year post-vaccination, a 45% reduction in H3N2 illness in the second year, and a 61% reduction in H1N1 illness in the third year post-vaccination. Serum hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) influenza antibodies and nasal IgA antibodies induced by vaccination with live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) remained detectable in children for more than one year after vaccination. In a community-based, nonrandomized, open-label trial, children who received a single dose of LAIV during the 1999-2000 influenza season demonstrated continued protection against medically attended acute respiratory illness (MAARI) during the 2000-2001 influenza season. A review of four trials (three randomized blinded and one open-label) involving children aged 6 months to 18 years reported that the efficacy of LAIV against influenza A (H1N1) and A (H3N2) was similar at 9-12 months post-vaccination compared to 1-<5 months post-vaccination. For influenza B strains, efficacy remained comparable at 5-7 months post-vaccination. Two randomized trials and one open-label study reported residual vaccine efficacy through a second influenza season without revaccination, although the efficacy was lower than that observed during the first season. Adults aged 65 years and older typically exhibit diminished immune responses to influenza vaccination compared to healthy younger adults. However, a review of published literature concluded that there is no clear evidence that vaccine-induced antibody levels decline more rapidly in the elderly. A case-control study conducted in Navarre, Spain, during the 2011-2012 influenza season showed a decline in vaccine effectiveness from 61% (95% CI: 5-84) during the first 100 days post-vaccination to 42% (95% CI: -39-75) between days 110-119, and to -35% (95% CI: -211-41) thereafter. This decline was most pronounced in individuals aged 65 years and older, where effectiveness dropped from 85% (95% CI: -8-98) to 24% (95% CI: -224-82) to -208% (95% CI: -1,563-43) over the same time intervals. However, most viruses isolated from infected vaccine recipients did not match the vaccine strains. Additionally, the wide confidence intervals surrounding these estimates suggest that larger studies are needed to better characterize the magnitude of potential declines in vaccine effectiveness over the season. Limited data suggest that administering additional vaccine doses during the same season does not enhance antibody responses among elderly vaccine recipients. Inactivated influenza vaccines (IIVs), which are administered via intramuscular or intradermal injection, contain non-replicating virus particles. Children aged 6 months and older typically develop protective antibody levels against specific influenza virus strains after receiving the recommended number of doses of seasonal IIV. Immunogenicity studies using the monovalent influenza A (H1N1) 2009 vaccine indicated that 80%-95% of vaccinated children developed protective antibody levels against the 2009 H1N1 virus after two doses. After one dose, the response was 50% in children aged 6-35 months and 75% in those aged 3-9 years. Studies involving seasonal IIV in young children have shown that two doses provide better protection than one dose during the first season a child is vaccinated. Vaccine effectiveness is lower among children under 5 years of age who have never been vaccinated before or who received only one dose in their first year of vaccination compared to those who received two doses in their first year. Two retrospective studies of children who received only one dose of IIV in their first year of vaccination found no reduction in influenza-like illness (ILI)-related office visits compared to unvaccinated children. Similar findings were reported in a case-control study of approximately 2,500 children aged 6-59 months, where laboratory-confirmed influenza was the outcome measure. These findings support the recommendation that all children aged 6 months to 8 years being vaccinated for the first time should receive two doses of influenza vaccine separated by at least four weeks. Vaccine effectiveness among children with chronic medical conditions is generally lower than that reported among healthy children. However, one study found that antibody responses in children with asthma are similar to those in healthy children and are not significantly altered during asthma exacerbations requiring short-term prednisone treatment.
